description.narrative: IISS has submitted a request for core support towards the implementation of its strategy (2021 - 2025) for the next four years. The strategy was developed based on the lessons learned from the previous strategy period (2017 - 2020) and is also informed by the changing peace and security dynamics in the continent. The process of adaptation to the existing COVID-19 context has also been reflected upon in the strategy document. For the strategy period 2021 - 2025, ISS has an overall goal to have evidence-based human security policies and practices is developed and implemented in Africa. The strategy has five outcome areas: - Decision makers on African human security and development challenges are informed by ISS research and analysis - Participants in ISS-convened dialogues & gatherings influence policy debates about human security challenges in Africa - Policies, strategies, programmes in key institutions dealing with Africa’s human security challenges are improved - Stakeholders’ capacity is built to effectively intervene with the aim of improving human security in Africa. - The ISS is an efficient and equitable employer, which develops its staff and encourages collaboration across offices and programmes. The strategy document also presents fourteen thematic topics including: African futures; Gender equality; Africa in the world; Governance, Peace and security; Democratic governance beyond elections; Capacity to prevent, manage and resolve conflicts and sustain peace; Youth peace and security; Maritime security; Migration and forced displacement; Security and governance of new technology; National and trans-national crime and violence; Violent extremism and counter- terrorism; Violence prevention; Criminal justice; and Climate change and human security.

description.narrative:
ISS has been providing UN Security Council discussion on the Sahel with analysis and policy advice. A report from the Dakar office was produced in June 2024 (Rethinking responses to unconstitutional changes of government in West Africa) and more than 70 briefings on transitions in Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso and Guinea has been delivered to regional governments, diplomats and international organisations. In addition, ISS has been delivered technical assistance to regional policing organisations has contributed to fostering regional networks that seek to tackle transnational organised crime, while fostering the licit movement of people, services and goods within regions to regional trade and integration. A third example of a result is the collaboration on the topic of maritime security among Western African coastal states. ISS has within this field provided knowledge and policy development regarding legislation and how West Africa's coastal states can develop cooperation in maritime security.
Sida assesses that the objectives will be achieved although it is not clearcut. On the positive side, Sida assesses that ISS is an organisation that: - Has adequate number of staff and competence to carry out the required work. - Has adequate mechanisms and procedures to reflect on and follow up on its programmes that also includes an ability to take decisions to adjust the work according to contextual developments. - Had adequate support process, networks and cooperations agreements with relevant organisations in order to carry out its tasks.
However, throughout the last two years, Sida has also noted a couple of challenges for ISS that can be summarized in the headings below:
Strategic coherence: Sida has noted that the activity base has broadened. Two examples of that are the national policy on violence prevention through parenting support" and "protecting South Africa's rare plants". They were emphasized as highlights in the outcome report for 2024, but were not further explained in the report. Although it is understood that these activities can belong to the broader realm of human security, it can be further explored and questioned how they relate and contribute to the general goal in the result matrix. Sida assesses that this broadening of the activity base risk diluting the core competence of ISS and that ISS takes on project grants in order to increase the funding which in some cases challenge the strategic coherence of the organisation.
Processes, partnerships and institutional relations: Sida understands that ISS contributes in various ways and capacities to different processes, builds and contributes to relationships with a broad range of actors. The reporting is mainly based on activities and for the future it would be worthwhile to also explore and find ways of reporting on processes, partnerships and institutional relationship. This also includes understanding and explaining the view and expectations of the participants that in various ways and capacities contribute. Sida assesses that a research based organisation would arguable be more skilled in explaining what kind of processes its human resources contribute to. There are many briefs, research papers, conferences and other activities that are produced. How these outputs relate to a demand remain sometimes unanswered. An exception to this is the work that ISS has contributed to in the maritime security of Western African. There was a realization among coastal West African states that there is a lack a coordinated response to martime threats. In this case, ISS could convene and contribute with its research skills to do practical work that was in demand by the coastal states.
Sida has noted that the current description of the impact "Evidence based human security policies and practices developed and implemented in Africa" does not capture the extent of how ISS works in processes and with relationships to achieve results. Relationship building and participation in political processes form a central part of the ISS activities. How this can be reflected in a possible future result matrix would be a topic for discussion.
Competing or harmonized demands?: How to liaise the requirements and expectations from being an institution, what does that mean in relation to also having requirements on resultbased management. Are there some activities that needs to be done as part of being an institution and how does that relate to the requirements of a result based organisation? On one hand, ISS wants to see itself as an instituions and on the other hand, it is subjected to the realities of result based management. This means that research and other activities need to follow the logic of result based management.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
